utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Unfortunately Judge Thelin is not here, so that Judge Van Den Wyngaert and I will sit. I'm glad that Mr. Radic has been able to join us. Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May I just deal with two matters, which can cut down today's hearing, I hope, in time. There is a schedule, I think, which the Court should have. The final document relates to 65 ter number 977 in respect of what I will call a journalistic interview with Mr. Sljivancanin. I just hold it up to assist the Court. I've spoken to my learned friend, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, you're referring to a schedule. What is it that you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have a document of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. And I hope, if Your Honour looks to the bottom, there is the 65 ter 977.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I just want to deal with that document. Ms. Regue will deal with all the others. I have had an opportunity of speaking to Mr. Lukic, and the agreement between us is quite simply this: That should Mr. Sljivancanin give evidence that we would not be estopped from cross-examining on this document, that he has now notice of the document itself. And so consequently there need not be any additional argument about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you don't press its admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So that should certainly clarify that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The second matter relates to General Pringle's report. It was footnote 4, from memory, which is Major-General Zorc's report. We submitted that it should be admissible and should be adduced as evidence of the truth of its content, which was adopted by General Pringle. I would wish to make a very short application in relation to that, oral application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic seems concerned about something. But I will do it just quickly, and it's this: That General Pringle is in a specific position as an expert. He had an opportunity of assessing the document itself. He gave evidence in relation to it by way of comparison and to some extent authenticating it in the sense that he considered it was comparable to the command and control doctrine that applies when -- in other arguments. My learned friend Mr. Vasic says they are disadvantaged because they are unable to cross-examine. Apart from the fact that my learned friend did cross-examine on one part of the document, we would submit that firstly it is admissable, its weight is a matter for the Court, an inability to cross-examine is not necessarily fatal, and in any event, with the fact that Major Pringle or Major-General Pringle adopted the report, the defence were therefore able to cross-examine Pringle on it in relation to other matters and as such, it should be admitted and the Court give it the appropriate weight as they -- as they see fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is wrong with the proposition, Mr. Moore, that insofar as the witness called adopted and relied upon the report, that has been the subject of his specific evidence, both oral and his written report, and has been in some respects at least the subject of cross-examination. Beyond that, the report of General Zorc has not featured in this trial. It's only insofar as it's been adopted and used by General Pringle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour has put it more eloquently than I. But that was exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But that would lead to the opposite result. It would lead to the report of Zorc not being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, not necessarily in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I'm putting to you that proposition, you see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, I would submit that that is not necessarily the case. That for a court to consider Pringle's replies in relation to that cross-examination, they should have the source material to assess the credibility or otherwise of that reply and of that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But you have chosen not to call that witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- that would have provided that source.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You want it to go in just because General Pringle has referred to one passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: He certainly didn't merely rely on one passage, he relied on the report, with regard to command and control, which is probably the most important part of General Pringle's evidence. So it's not a case of just one passage. If, however, Your Honour takes the view that the Prosecution should have called General Zorc and therefore that is fatal to the report itself, then of course that is the Court's prerogative. But we would submit that for any expert or any expert's evidence to be evaluated, the Court should always have an opportunity of assessing the source material. And in this case the source material has been available to the Defence, and they have been able to cross-examine Pringle on the part that he adopted. So they have not been disadvantaged, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But you somehow want to leap from that to tendering the whole of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would seek to tender the report on relevant aspects. For example, that report dealt with Dubrovnik. One would obviously not deal with those areas. And I'm quite happy to put a pen through paragraphs that we would not seek to rely upon. But where Pringle says in relation to command and control that I see Zorc, his report on it, and I consider it to be analogous to, as in his case, the British military forces, then in our submission that is a matter that the Court are entitled to look at and to evaluate as a question of, firstly, weight in relation to Zorc, and Zorc's report, and, secondly, the credibility of Pringle's evidence on that material. I wouldn't put the matter any higher than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I just deal with the General Zorc situation. I would like to leave court if it is as all possible. There is one further administrative matter that I would wish to deal with. I wonder if Your Honour could hear me on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's quite simply this: Clearly there are 98 bis arguments to come. It would assist certainly the Prosecution if the Defence would be able to either indicate the documents that they would seek to rely upon in the 98 bis argument, and/or the counts to which they would make suppressions. And if that could be done, that would be extremely helpful. There's no obligation for them to do so, but it is not perhaps an unreasonable request in relation to the case as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, can I say, Mr. Moore, that I have no doubt that it would be of assistance to you, and I have no doubt that if your learned friends on the opposite side are in a position to do so, that they would, in the spirit that has been shown in this trial, let you have that information, but I don't think that it's a case where this Chamber should make a ruling to require that that be done at this point. Bearing in mind the nature of 98 bis, at least as it's now been clarified by the amended Rule, in your jurisdiction and mine you would be rather used to, I would think, as you sat down having closed your case, to the equivalent of 98 bis being moved on the spot orally and your response orally on the spot, and a decision, if not on the spot, by the next morning, orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: In a case of perhaps one or two weeks, the answer would be yes, but not a case of this size. Normally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not so?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh, dear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Perhaps they're much more able in Australia than mortals in Britain. But normally in a case of this size we would have a general indication of what the submissions would be not extensively in any way at all, but firstly to deal with the counts, and perhaps - dreadful phrase - bullet points, so that the Chamber or the Court and all parties would know exactly where they stand. So that would be the position in our jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it's interesting. Is it possible for Defence counsel to indicate whether they will be in the position to give advance notice to Mr. Moore of their 98 bis submissions? Yes or no would do, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I'm afraid the answer is no. We would be submitting such information to our learned friend in case the Defence had a crystal clear, or rather clear-cut position already that we were aware of, which seems not to be the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you speak for all counsel, I take it? Very well. There's your answer, Mr. Moore. Looking ahead to Wednesday, the Chamber had felt that it should indicate a general timetable for the day for the submissions. We would expect that the submissions of each accused might be dealt with in between half and three-quarters of an hour. They may well be able to be put in a shorter period than that, but we want to indicate the outside limit, so that preparations can proceed on that basis. Which would mean at the worst, for time, that Mr. Vasic would have from 9.30 to 10.15, Mr. Borovic from 10.30 -- 10.15 to 11.00, and Mr. Lukic from 11.20 to 12.05. We would think in deference to Mr. Moore's concerns that we should not then proceed until the afternoon to hear his response. And as he's dealing with all three cases, that he might have up to an hour to respond. So that would be 2.15 -- no, it's the other time table, isn't it. 1345 to 1445. I think 1345 to 1445, Mr. Moore. And it will then be by then possible for the Chamber to know whether it can give its decision on the afternoon of Wednesday or whether it will be necessary to give a decision on Friday, as we are all of Thursday, in a Plenary, and not able to sit on Thursday. But it -- we'll decide once we've heard the submissions and been able to consult with each other whether we can give a decision on Wednesday or whether it will be Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you then, Mr. Moore. Ms. Regue,

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I will seek to tender only 10 documents from the bar table instead of 11. And well, we will start with the first indictment from the Belgrade prosecutor, number 3/03, dated the 4th of December, 2003. The ERN number, both in English and in B/C/S, is 0345-2550-0345-2563.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: We will seek to tender these documents with regards to the name of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, is there any difference of admissibility between documents 1, 2 and ...

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: 1 and 2, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Only 1 and 2, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was going to explain that. Actually, there are two indictments. There was an initial indictment, the 4th of December, 2003, where eight accused were indicted, and then the trial started but investigations continued. And then a second indictment was issued the 25th of May, 2004 against 11 accused. With regard to the first indictment, one accused committed suicide for your information. And we seek to tender both indictments because they actually include all the accused which are in the judgement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Are there any particular further submissions you want to put?

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are there any other particular submissions you want to put as to why they should be received.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. We seek to show actually that the accused which are mentioned in this indictment were the physical perpetrators in the Ovcara crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there in objection? Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, only in relation to what my learned friend has just suggested; namely, that the Prosecutor is tendering this document in order to prove that the people mentioned here are the physical perpetrators of the crime at Ovcara. I don't think that can be based on the indictment, because the indictment is not a document which you can use to establish something like that. A final judgement might be, but not the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Borovic, any submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've given my argument in relation to the first-instance judgement. That is based on the indictments. I think that proposal was sufficient, what the Chamber told the OTP, that such a judgement can be tendered, but that the Chamber can only realise what the nature of the judgement is, once it has been announced as final by the relevant Trial Chamber. That still seems to be my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I support what my learned friends have said so far. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, documents 3, 4, 5 and 6, Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You don't wish me to actually read out the ERN numbers of indictment number 2? It's not necessary?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's no need to read them out.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks, Your Honour. Document number 3 is the B/C/S transcript of the audio recording of the Ovcara judgement of the Belgrade war crimes court dated 12th December, 2005. As we actually expressed last week, Mr. Moore expressed in the courtroom, we seek to tender the judgement only with regards to the verdict or to the judgement. And for us the relevance of these documents is to show that the accused or in this case the accused who were pronounced guilty were indeed physical perpetrators in the Ovcara crime. It has been put by some witness in this case. And Your Honours, the document number 4, I won't read, as you indicated the ERN number, is the English translation of the transcript, of the audio recording. Document number 5 is the judgement itself. Because in Belgrade actually the written judgement doesn't become public until some time. So what we obtained right away, it was only the audio recording, the transcript of the audio recording, which was a summary of the December public hearing. And we obtained very recently only the complete judgement. And we will tender right now the judgement itself in B/C/S for the same purposes as the hearing, as the transcript. And once we obtain the English translation, we will seek to tender the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Document number 6 is the transcript of the audio recording of another judgement pronounced against Milan Bulic. If I may explain, Your Honour, in Belgrade there were three Ovcara proceedings running at the same time. The main Ovcara case, which was -- the judgement was pronounce in December, there was another trial against Milan Bulic, who was charged for the same crimes, but for illness he was separated from the other perpetrators. And his judgement was actually read out the 30th of January, and we just obtained very recently the transcript of the hearing. So we seek to tender actually the transcript of the hearing only read out the verdict. There is still an ongoing trial proceeding against another accused called Sasa Radak which was arrested at a later stage. So this proceeding is still ongoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And if this were admitted, you would seek, in due course, so supplement what is there with an English translation?

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as soon as we obtain the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Again, I have the same concern as earlier on. We have this judgement of the special court in Belgrade, I don't think this document can be used as evidence to show that these people indeed committed the war crime that they were convicted for. This is not a final judgement. All we can say is that this non-final judgement, as it were, says they're guilty. The weight of this particular piece of evidence very much depends on what the Appeals Chamber decides to do. It depends on whether they decide to amend the original document, whether they perhaps decide to acquit or throw the entire case out and send them all back to square one, depending, of course, on all the evidence placed before the Trial Chamber. It is in this sense that I believe this document can be tendered, but its weight as evidence is limited at best. There is a first-instance ruling or judgement containing a guilty verdict, but we use remember that this is not a final judgement. As for the transcripts of the audio recordings, from the reading of the judgement, they might be authentic, but under our laws they represent to me a summary of the judgement, the reasons for the judgement being stated in brief, and then this is followed by a more detailed account of the reasoning behind the judgement. This document is limited in its scope, and I hardly believe it could prove of any use, since you have the judgement itself to read. The same arguments apply to everything else that my learned friend has been seeking to tender. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Your Honour -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will be very brief. As a matter of principle, disputing a non-final judgement is perfectly justifiable. I believe our learned friends from the OTP understand that, even bearing in mind the fact that all those indicted denied their responsibility. Perhaps if someone takes a look at some of those statements, I believe that might be helpful for my client, precisely for the same legal qualifications that have been presented here in this case. I would not like to go too far into that now though. As a matter of principle, I leave it to the Chamber to rule whether this can be accepted as evidence admitted into evidence or not. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I support what my learned friends have said, but there is another objection that I wish to raise at this juncture. As for the written summary of the judgement, we were given a copy today for the first time. This contains 137 pages in the B/C/S original. I saw it today when I came to the courtroom for the very first time. We need time to have a look and to see what our position is. What I'm trying to say, in other words, is this document is entirely new to us, and we have never seen it before. I have scan-read the document, and I have seen numerous references to numerous statements in the document. Therefore, I believe I need some more time to be able to give the Chamber a more articulate or final position on this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Lukic, does that not ignore the nature of this document? It's a judgement of a court. Whether it's an interim, final or whatever type of judgement, it is an interim judgement. Necessarily that will be dealing with the evidence that was presented to the court, and the court's views about it. How will it affect the admissibility of that document for you to want to explore for your own purposes all the evidence that the court relied on?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One thing that just occurred to me, it is possible that our own clients' statements are quoted in this document, because their statements were read at trial. Are these statements fit to become evidence? They might as well be tendered through a document like that. I just want to go through this judgement to see whether anything is quoted in the judgement that we believe to be unfit to be admitted into evidence. The weight of the judgement is something else. That is up to the Chamber to decide. The reason I'm objecting, and the reason I am proposing that this merely be marked for identification, is I believe it is my duty to go through this document thoroughly to see what's in it, or rather if there might be something in it that we deem to be inadmissible. That's my position right now, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honours. Just concerning this last point, Mr. Lukic. We actually disclosed the judgement, I have with me here the receipt, June 16. So actually the Defence had with them the judgement since June 16, so they had -- we didn't give to them the document today, we disclosed to them the document, if I'm correct, like one week and a half ago. So we disclosed that document earlier on. It's not like today that they gave the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was a rather busy week.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yeah, but it's not today we gave the document, Your Honour. And also, Your Honour, just to clarify what we already stated last week, we don't seek to tender all the judgement. We seek to tender only the document concerning the name -- the indictment concerning the names of the accused and also the verdict. So not the full judgement itself, only the verdict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do we misunderstand you then? I thought you were seeking to tender the full judgement. That's what's described here.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yeah, we seek to tender the full judgement, but only concerning the verdict. Meaning the accused. The people who are -- who are actually declared accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: See, Mr. Lukic is worried about what might lie within all these pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Okay. So maybe he will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Whereas if you were simply saying we want to go to the verdict at the end, the conclusion and only that, that's quite different from the whole judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: So I think that, Your Honour, what we were put in front of the Trial Chamber last week, that's what Mr. Moore actually was putting to the Trial Chamber last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will the whole of the transcript and the English translation of the pronouncement of judgement --

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know what would be in that without looking at it. And then the whole of the written judgement. I assume that included the full reasons for decision. Am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Can you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The procedure may be a little different in Serbia. But, for example, here, if we should ever come to give a decision at the end of this trial on the guilt or innocence of the accused, there might be a document of 50 or 100 or more pages in which we set out the issues, the legal points, the essential facts, our findings based on those facts, and then we come to say, has each accused been proved guilty of each of the offences. And in the end we then say, in our verdict, we find accused X guilty of counts this or that, and not guilty of some others.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The whole of the decision is our judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But the verdict is only a very small part of it where we say guilty or not guilty.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: But Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, is that differentiation what we're dealing with here or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: I'm afraid it is, Your Honours. We were actually seeking to tender only this portion of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to help my learned friend a little bit. I think that she has proposed a good thing, just to tender the verdict. In that case, the position of the Defence would be different. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because Judge Thelin is not here today, and because this is a decision which we would want to discuss with all three Judges, we will not give a decision today. We would hope to give a decision on this matter on Wednesday, when we assemble for the 98 bis arguments. Could I suggest, Ms. Regue, that you discuss with Defence counsel, when we adjourn today, just what parts of the judgements and the transcripts you want to tender, if it is that you can then agree, as Mr. Borovic has hinted, that certain parts only, being what I might call the verdict, are to be tendered, it may be that they can be tendered with the agreement of Defence counsel, and if that is the position, that could be indicated to the Chamber by a short memorandum, and we will then be in the position to admit it on Wednesday. If you are not able to reach agreement, we will proceed on the basis that what is being proposed to be tendered is the full transcript of the proceedings when the judgement was delivered and the full judgement as it's been published. If you want something else, you'd better notify us in writing before Wednesday. Is that clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yeah, it's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Document 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is a Human Rights Watch report, name war crimes in the former Yugoslavia, 65 ter document 198. And for the Prosecution the relevance of this document is that it goes to the wide-spread and systematic element in larger parts of Croatia, including the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any objection? No objection. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 602.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: The following document is the report on the battle for Vukovar from Mr. Cherif Bassiouni and others. It's 65 ter document 285 dated 14th October 1993. The relevance of this document also goes to the wide-spread and systematic element in Mr. -- in Slavonia, including the municipality of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is there any objection? That will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 603.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Document number 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The other document has the ERN number 0007-2605. It's part of the 65 ter document 288. It's the -- a letter from the British Medical Association to the General Kadijevic. And for the Prosecution this document goes for notice of the crimes committed in Vukovar. It's dated 9th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Any objection? It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 604.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And the last document is also part of the 65 ter document 288. And the B/C/S -- excuse me, the ERN in English is 0007-2602-0007-2604. And it's a letter from Amnesty International to the government of Croatia. And the relevance of this document, it also actually goes for notice concerning the crimes committed in Vukovar, and it's dated 27th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Any objection? It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 605, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. REGUE
utterances.text: And finally, Your Honour, Mr. Weiner has one document to offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Regue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Document number MFI 345, which is the blue folder, it's been marked for identification since April 4th of this year. It is a list of persons who received treatment at the Vukovar Hospital and were later killed at Ovcara and raises an inference that they were patients on November 18th through 20th. There's been testimony about the document through Dr. Bosanac, Dr. Kostovic, as well as the 89(F) statement of Dr. Kostovic discusses the accuracy and the contents of the document. Now, out of the 3500 or so notations in there, last week counsel indicated through their cross-examination that there were a handful of errors. But if we look at that, out of 35 or so hundred, five errors is much less than one per cent. In fact, in the Tuta Stela case, the Prosecutor against Naletilic and Martinovic, the decision on the admission of exhibits tendered through Witness Mladen Ancic, which is 4 October 2002, they note that the fact that a document is accepted into evidence does not mean that it is fully accurate. And that's on page 3 where the Court says: "Considering furthermore that the mere admission of a document does not necessarily mean that the document gives an accurate portrayal of the facts." There can be some errors in there, and in this case we would argue that it is a very small amount of errors. But based on the Tuta Stela case, which cites other matters, that -- the fact of a few errors is not determinative on the issue of admissibility. Now, the documents which this blue folder is based on were admitted through Dr. Kostovic. All those statistics and documents from the Vukovar Hospital that were sent to Zagreb in Exhibits 596, 597 and 598. Now, those documents can be used to corroborate the so-called blue folder, which is document 345, or can be used as a comparison to ensure accuracy. So based on the other documents that have been admitted, the testimony and the 89(F) exhibit of Dr. Kostovic, we would ask that the blue folder, which has been mentioned many times in this case, be admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vasic. It looks as though you've been volunteered, Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Good afternoon. Since I already spoke on the subject of the admissibility of Exhibit 345, in its status of MFI, I wanted to now respond to the suggestion of my learned friend. At the beginning, he mentioned that this was a document which was actually a list of patients of the Vukovar Hospital who were killed at Ovcara later. The document itself states, and this was established through other evidence, that from number -- from the number of persons cited in the annex to the indictment we have 14 persons who were exhumed in some other location, so that it cannot, with certainty, be asserted that those persons were also killed at Ovcara. The blue folder is something that has been discussed a lot on several occasions. That piece of evidence was used in the examination of several witnesses. I would just like to remind the Trial Chamber that when the document was presented for the first time this was in April of this year, shortly before the second appearance of Dr. Vesna Bosanac before this Trial Chamber, when Mr. Moore from the Prosecution also discussed this at your request. And your instruction then, Your Honours, was, and I will read it out. It's on page 7276 of the transcript. "[Previous translation continues] ... [In English] If they are available, those source documents, in respect of the persons in the indictment ..." [B/C/S spoken] "[In English] ... should be made available to the Defence." In the cross-examination, and even during re-examination of Dr. Vesna Bosanac, we saw that she said that the document 345 was drafted on the basis of information stored in Zagreb. Even though your instruction was to make these documents available to the Defence, we did not receive the documents on which this particular exhibit is based. If we also look at the examination-in-chief by Mr. Moore of Dr. Vesna Bosanac, we also can see that the blue folder was printed on the basis of a table provided to the Prosecution on a compact disc by Dr. Vesna Bosanac, and as far as I can recall, the Defence received this exhibit in December during the Christmas recess. That's the document, if you recall, which is quite large. It's a very big table, with 32 vertical columns, and obviously the blue folder was made by breaking up this large table made by the ministry, the sector for information, and it was made by the Prosecution then and offered here as an exhibit as a document which is practically being offered by Dr. Vesna Bosanac for reasons cited during the cross-examination of Dr. Kostovic, where basically it was confirmed in the view of the Defence, all three Defence teams, it was confirmed that the documents or the names of the accused from the basic list, which is actually the main, or the basic, the source document of the ministry, the sector for information based on which Dr. Bosanac's analysis and documents were derived, we see that the facts do not quite tally, and for those reasons this document is not acceptable, because we were not given access to the source information based on which the whole database was made, were not also informed about the methodology in which the -- the database of the blue folder was drafted. So for these reasons, this folder is not -- this exhibit is not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I accept what my colleague has stated. We all recall these particulars that she talked about. I would just like to touch upon one thing that my learned friend, Mr. Weiner, stated in his request to have this document admitted. He said that the Prosecution, on the basis of this document, wishes to prove that these persons were being treated at the hospital from the 18th to the 20th of November, 1991, and that after that they were killed at Ovcara. I believe that this document is inappropriate to establish something like this. Your Honours, you will recall that from the statements of Mrs. Bosanac and Mr. Kostovic, and even Mr. Strinovic, we learned that the entire documentation, based on which this list was drafted, at least according to what they said, there was no record of the discharge of patients from the Vukovar Hospital. So it cannot be established on the basis of this document how long each patient spent at the hospital, what sort of medical treatment they received, and when each of them was discharged. Perhaps this could be a document of people who had passed through the hospital in one way or another, but we don't know when they were admitted, when they were discharged. And for us it is of key interest to establish whether a patient was at the hospital in the period from the 18th to the 20th, were they being provided with treatment at that time, and then were they released after treatment or not -- discharged after treatment or not. During the examination of Mr. Kostovic, we found out that only at the beginning of the armed conflict and during the reports sent from Vukovar, records were maintained about the day patients, and only in this initial phase was it indicated who was admitted as a day patient or who wasn't. This documentation was not maintained later. So based on this list, we cannot see who was actually admitted and who was treated as a day patient. And finally we cannot see from this list whether a person was readmitted to the hospital several times, because we don't know when they were discharged. In only one instance is their data about a person being admitted twice. That was actually the duty of input of those who maintained these records. Just like my colleague Ms. Tapuskovic said, the Prosecution was not able to verify the incomplete data on the basis of which the report was drafted, according to what Mr. Kostovic says. And we believe that this document is not an appropriate document to prove the assertions that the Prosecution wishes to prove.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing. I agree with everything my colleagues have said, and I would like to add one small argument to decide on the suitability of this document. As I recall during the cross-examination of Mr. -- Ms. Tapuskovic of Mr. Kostovic, he said that the accuracy was something that he was not able to verify and was not something that he did that. So he used, or he drafted his reports without verifying the authenticity of the sources. And also on top of that we were not able to see these source documents, which leads us to the conclusion that the report, the way it is, is not suitable to be admitted as an exhibit. We're not talking about the weight of the document or its probative value, but we believe that a document drafted in this way is something that is not suitable to prove the assertions that are -- that it is the intention of the Prosecution to prove through this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour. Two points. One, with regard to the source of the information, if the Court looks to April 3rd, page 7053, and a few pages before that and after that, the information here comes from a CD. The CD was provided by Dr. Bosanac. She received the information from the Ministry of Health, meaning Dr. Kostovic. Dr. Kostovic has testified. He has provided the information to her in 1997. Number two, as a further source of information we provided through Dr. Kostovic at least three different exhibits where he gives -- shows the copies of information that was received from Vukovar, that he received from Vukovar, be it from the MUP or the hospital. So we have provided the source of this information. And with regard to the CD, the initial provision of the CD was as early as December of 2005. And just finally, we are offering this document to establish an inference, not a presumption, but an inference with regard to those particular patients. And we'd suggest that the evidence is sufficient to establish that inference and to have the document admitted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may speak, Your Honours. Thank you. My colleague from the Prosecution only confirmed what we stressed, and that is that the CD with the data was received in December. But this is a document that does not contain a single name of a single patient for reasons that were noted by Vesna Bosanac and our colleague, Mr. Moore, that had to do with the privacy or confidentiality of witnesses who were being given treatment, medical treatment. So the document being tendered has some names, but not all the names of the persons that are mentioned in the annex to the indictment. We cannot establish, with absolute certainty the correlation between document 345 and the document that was disclosed to us on the compact disc. As my colleague, Mr. Lukic [realtime transcript read in error "Vasic"] said, Witness Kostovic affirmed or confirmed that the accuracy of the data received from the hospital could not have been verified, but this data was entered. By saying this to Witness Kostovic, we saw that the information from the MUP dispatches is different from the data entered in the blue folder. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one technical matter. On page 25, line 23, my learned friend spoke about what Mr. Lukic said, whereas the transcript says Vasic. So there's a slight error there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You want to disown it do you, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This will be the subject of our decision on Wednesday as well. Any other matter to be raised by any counsel? Very well. Can we thank you for your assistance today. And we will resume sitting at 9.30 on Wednesday morning. We now adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 28th day of June, 2006, at 9.30 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.36 p.m.,
